extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of moral philosophy / ethics (Aristotelian virtue ethics)
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and summarizing the criteria Aristotle gives for what counts as Friendship, the kinds of Friendship, and related moral requirements (self-love, benefaction, number/needs of friends, unity of sentiment).

rubrics_metrics.name: Friend as one who intends and does good for another for that other's sake
rubrics_metrics.description: A friend is 'one who intends and does what is good (or what he believes to be good) to another for that other's sake.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This formulation stresses motive (for the other's sake) and action (does what is good). Examples: the feeling of mothers towards their children; friends who come into collision. Anti-pattern: acts done for self-interest or advantage are not true friendship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Friend as one who wishes another to be and live for that other's own sake
rubrics_metrics.description: A friend is 'one who wishes his friend to be and to live for that friend's own sake.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasizes wanting the friend's well‑being intrinsically (not instrumentally). Used to distinguish genuine friendship from relationships based on use or pleasure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Friend as fellow in life and common choices / sympathiser in joys and sorrows
rubrics_metrics.description: Friendship may be characterised as 'one who lives with another and chooses the same objects,' or 'one who sympathises with his friend in his sorrows and in his joys.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focuses on shared life, shared aims and emotional sympathy. Such sympathising and shared pursuits are marks of intimacy; contrasted with superficial liking or mere acquaintanceship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Friendship as another Self (self-like unity)
rubrics_metrics.description: The good man has towards himself the same marks that constitute friendship, and a friend is in fact 'another Self.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle uses the self-friendship of the good man as the paradigm: unity of desire, consistent choice of the good, and mutual sympathy. This supplies a standard: true friendship resembles the attitudes one has toward a well-ordered self.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity of desires and consistency as requirement for friendship
rubrics_metrics.description: Friendship presupposes unity: 'he is at unity in himself, and with every part of his soul he desires the same objects; and he wishes for himself both what is, and what he believes to be, good; and he does it.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criterion: concordance between belief, desire and action. Anti-pattern: persons at variance within themselves (lack of self-control, remorseful wicked) cannot sustain friendship with themselves or others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wickedness (internal faction) prevents friendship
rubrics_metrics.description: Those who are depraved, villainous, or at variance with themselves cannot be friends even with themselves, because they lack the unity and pleasant self-recollection that produce friendly sentiments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: those who prefer hurtful pleasures, the cowardly or indolent who avoid what is best; those who have committed dreadful actions and flee themselves. Such characters cannot sympathise with their selves, so they lack friendship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Kindly Feeling (philia) vs Friendship (mature philia)
rubrics_metrics.description: Kindly Feeling resembles friendship but is not identical: it may exist toward persons unaware of it, lacks intensity/yearning and intimacy, and may be a 'dormant Friendship' that sometimes ripens into real Friendship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kindly Feeling is the starting point of Friendship (analogous to sight-pleasure as the start of love) but does not imply commitment to action or sacrifice. Anti-pattern: kindly feeling motivated by advantage or pleasure does not produce genuine kindly feeling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity of Sentiment (social friendship) concerns action and mutual advantage
rubrics_metrics.description: Unity of Sentiment is agreement 'respecting points of expediency and [taking] the same line and carry[ing] out what has been determined in common consultation.' It is not mere unity of opinion (e.g., on astronomy).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This social unity governs common action (e.g., choosing magistrates or alliances) and is characteristic of communities and friendships oriented to the common good. Among the good it is steady; among the bad it fails, leading to quarrels and neglect of the common good.

rubrics_metrics.name: Benefactors commonly feel more Friendship for beneficiaries
rubrics_metrics.description: Benefactors are commonly held to have more Friendship for the objects of their kindness than these for them; Aristotle explains this by likening the benefactor's affection to love of one's own work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reasons given: creators 'exist' by their acts of working and therefore love their works; honour endures for the benefactor while advantage to recipient is fleeting; labor invested increases attachment. Example: poets loving their poems; mothers' special fondness due to labor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between vulgar self-love and proper self-love
rubrics_metrics.description: The term 'self-loving' is used disparagingly for those who seek more than their share of wealth, honours, and bodily pleasures (vulgar self-love). In contrast, proper self-love is loving and obeying the rational/intellectual principle (the highest part of the soul) and securing the noblest goods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criterion: whether one pursues low, passionate goods (blameworthy) or the noble/kalon (praiseworthy). The good man is 'most truly Self-loving' in the sense of cherishing the rational principle and virtuous actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good man's self-love is virtuous and grounds friendship
rubrics_metrics.description: Because the good man loves the rational principle and does noble acts (which benefit himself and others), he is properly self-loving and thereby fitted to be a friend to others and to himself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: the good man may sacrifice money, honours, or life for friends or country because such acts secure the kalon (the noble) to himself; giving to a friend can reflect honour on the giver—thus benefiting the self in the proper sense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Happy man does need friends (contrary to some views)
rubrics_metrics.description: Although some argue that the blessed/independent man has no need of friends because he has all goods, Aristotle argues the Happy man nevertheless needs friends—for benefactions to exercise virtue, companionship, and the pleasure of contemplating good actions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clarifies types of friends: the happy man will not need friends merely useful for material advantage, but will need friends as objects for virtuous action and for companionship in living and working (friend as second Self).

rubrics_metrics.name: Number of friends limited by possibility of intimacy
rubrics_metrics.description: One should not have exceedingly many friends: the limit is 'the greatest number with whom it would be possible to keep up intimacy.' Intimacy and mutual friendship among the group are required, and it is difficult to be intimate with many.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern: having many acquaintances without true intimacy; over-complaisant characters who seem friends to many but are truly friends to none. Practical rule: have enough friends for intimacy, not a large number of superficial friends.

rubrics_metrics.name: Friends are more necessary in adversity than in prosperity
rubrics_metrics.description: Friends are required in both states, but more necessary in adversity because the unfortunate need help; in prosperity friends are more honoured and are objects for the good man's benefactions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prescriptive behavior: call friends readily in prosperity (to confer benefits) but be cautious about imposing misfortunes on friends; go to friends in their misfortunes unasked and eagerly to render assistance. Note mixed effects of friends' presence: comfort and possible additional pain if friends share the suffering.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intimacy and shared activity are the essence of Friendship (communion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Intimacy (communal life and sharing in what each values) is the chief thing prized by friends; friends 'spend their days together in that which they like best of all things in life'—drinking, studying, hunting, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Friendship of the good improves both parties through repeated acts and mutual correction ('Thou from the good, good things shalt surely learn'). Anti-pattern: friendship among the wicked corrupts them by making them alike in vice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pleasure's role in moral education and its contested status as Chief Good
rubrics_metrics.description: Pleasure is closely bound with our kind and used in training the young (rudders of Pleasure and Pain); some (Eudoxus) call Pleasure the Chief Good because all beings aim at it, while others condemn it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criterion for moral formation: learning to like and dislike what one ought is crucial. Aristotle warns against merely doctrinaire rejection of pleasure and favors accounts that fit facts and life. This opens a standard for evaluating claims about pleasure's primacy in a good life.
